meta.name: Bucket Test
meta.purpose: Route respondent into one of 13 ideological family buckets via 6 structural axes. Cultural axis is measured but NEVER used for routing.

scoring.formula: raw[axis] = sum(mult * effect[axis]); max[axis] = sum(abs(effect[axis])); score[axis] = 100 * (max + raw) / (2 * max)
scoring.note: Positive effect pulls toward the SECOND pole named in the axis label. Every axis is keyed-balanced: positive-keyed magnitudes sum exactly equal to negative-keyed magnitudes, so an all-neutral respondent lands at exactly 50 on every axis.

routing.description: Compute Euclidean distance between the respondent's 6-axis vector and each bucket anchor vector below. Lowest distance wins. Report the top 3 with match percentages so near-ties are visible.
routing.anchorsStatus: v0.2 - retuned. Min pairwise separation 36.1 (was 15.0). Monte Carlo self-routing at sigma=15 noise: 86.1% (was 78.2%).

designRules: Axis-pure: no question loads onto more than one routing axis. Keeps the distance metric honest and makes misroutes debuggable.
Keyed-balanced: half the items on each axis are reverse-keyed, to control acquiescence bias.
Graded weights (7-10), not a flat 10 like 8values. Weaker discriminators carry less.
No consensus statements. Every item should split respondents; if nearly everyone agrees, it carries no information.

Legitimacy measures the SOURCE OF POLITICAL AUTHORITY (divine law vs human law), never personal piety or cultural conservatism. This is 8values' single biggest design error - it fused religion and traditionalism into one axis.
Cultural axis is a separate appendage stat, orthogonal by design, excluded from all routing math.
meta.presentation: Questions are stored grouped by axis for maintainability. The app should SHUFFLE them (fixed seed for reproducible share-links) so consecutive items don't come from the same axis - grouped presentation invites response sets.

questions.text: A single disciplined organisation must hold decisive power during a period of transformation.
Political opposition can legitimately be banned when it threatens the established order.
The state is right to use surveillance against organised internal enemies.
A centralised command structure is more effective than any assembly or council.
Ordinary people generally lack the information needed to decide major questions of state directly.
Coercion by the state is a normal instrument of rule, not a regrettable exception.
Discipline and obedience are more valuable civic qualities than dissent.
A single leader holding wide personal authority serves a country better than rule by committee.
All political power should be exercised by delegates who can be recalled at any moment.
No permanent body of officials should be allowed to exist above the population.
Any concentration of coercive power reproduces domination regardless of who holds it.
Decisions should be made by federated local assemblies rather than a central authority.
The right to organise politically must be unconditional, including for one's enemies.
Hierarchy within an organisation corrupts its purpose, however good its intentions.
A police apparatus separate from the armed population is always dangerous.
Rule by permanent officials is a form of class power in its own right.
A revolutionary movement needs a formal, disciplined party organisation even when it holds no state power.
Binding collective decisions are necessary; spontaneous coordination is not enough.
Any group should be free to ignore a decision it did not itself consent to.
Political authority should never be delegated to anyone, even temporarily.
Society took a wrong turn at an identifiable point in the past and should return to what preceded it.
Inherited institutions carry accumulated wisdom that no deliberate redesign can replace.
The transformations of the past century have been mostly losses to be reversed.
Restoring an older order is a more worthy aim than constructing a new one.
Continuity with our ancestors is a stronger claim on us than the demands of the future.
Attempts to remake society from first principles end in catastrophe.
The existing order should be defended against those who would overturn it.
Stability is worth more than justice when the two come into conflict.
The present order cannot be repaired and must be broken.
What is needed is a rupture with the entire existing structure, not a series of corrections.
Existing institutions should be dismantled rather than inherited and reformed.
Nothing in the present arrangement is worth conserving for its own sake.
Decisive change comes through struggle, not through legislation.
Gradual reform ultimately stabilises the thing it claims to improve.
History moves forward, and the task is to accelerate it.
Those who defend continuity are really defending the interests continuity serves.
The traditional family structure should be upheld as the social norm.
Established sexual morality should be maintained and publicly upheld.
Long-standing cultural and religious customs deserve deference even when they constrain individuals.
Changes in gender roles over recent decades have gone too far.
Individuals should be free to define their own identity and way of life without social sanction.
Inherited moral codes should be revised whenever they conflict with individual freedom.
Society should actively work to dismantle traditional social hierarchies in everyday life.
Public morality should keep pace with changing social attitudes rather than resist them.
Competition between privately owned firms is the most reliable engine of prosperity.
Wealth accumulated through business success is legitimately earned and should not be redistributed.
Price signals allocate resources better than any planning body could.
Passing private wealth to one's children across generations is legitimate.
Most industries currently in state hands would be run better privately.
The commanding heights of the economy — energy, transport, heavy industry — should be publicly owned.
Employment for wages is inherently exploitative, whatever the wage level.
Production should be organised to meet needs directly, not to be sold for profit.
The gap between the highest and lowest incomes should be capped by law.
Land should not be privately owned as a commodity.
Key industries should be taken into public ownership even when they are running profitably.
Workers should have a legally guaranteed share of control over the firms that employ them.
A well-regulated market economy with a strong welfare state is preferable to public ownership.
Redistributing income through taxation is preferable to changing who owns productive property.
A powerful state is entitled to secure its interests abroad by force.
Some nations are fit to lead others, and the world order should reflect this.
Territorial expansion is a legitimate expression of national vitality.
Military intervention abroad is justified when it serves the intervening nation's interests.
Great powers naturally have spheres of influence that smaller states must respect.
The wealth of the developed world rests on continued extraction of value from the periphery.
Armed resistance to foreign occupation is a legitimate response to illegitimate force.
A government that serves a foreign imperial power against its own people forfeits its legitimacy.
National liberation struggles in the periphery are a central front of world politics, not a peripheral concern.
Sanctions and debt are instruments of domination as much as armies are.
Political authority is ultimately answerable to divine law, not to any human assembly.
Legislation that contradicts revealed law is illegitimate regardless of how it was passed.
Religious scholars should hold formal power to review the state's decisions.
A state without a religious foundation cannot command genuine obedience.
Public life should be ordered according to a single revealed moral code.
The clergy are a more trustworthy check on rulers than any constitution.
Religious institutions should be funded and privileged by the state.
A sacred order stands above politics and sets its limits.
Law derives its authority solely from human beings, and from nothing above them.
Religious institutions should have no formal role in government whatsoever.
Religious teaching is too often used to make people accept injustice they would otherwise resist.
The state should treat all metaphysical claims as private matters with no political standing.
Political questions should be settled by material analysis, not by scripture.
A religious ruling class is a ruling class like any other.
Public policy should never appeal to divine sanction as its justification.
Clerical influence over the state should be actively removed where it exists.
The bonds between members of a nation matter more than the bonds between workers of different nations.
A people sharing common descent and culture is the natural political unit.
Loyalty to one's country should override loyalty to any international movement.
Conflict between classes within a nation is a distraction from the nation's common interest.
Large-scale immigration dissolves the solidarity a political community depends on.
A worker has more in common with a foreign worker than with an employer of their own nationality.
Nations are historical constructions that will dissolve as class society is overcome.
Appeals to a shared 'national interest' usually mask the particular interests of that nation's ruling class.
Borders serve mainly to divide those who would otherwise share a common interest.
Appeals to national unity are usually a means of suppressing internal conflict.
